messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 68
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Unemployed
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Sleeping Alone: Sleeping alone or in an unfamiliar place, Feeling Vulnerable: Feeling emotionally vulnerable, Olfactory (Earth/Outdoor): Soil or outdoor smells
  Maladaptive Strategies: People Pleasing: go along with whatever others want to feel safe, Busyness: I work hard at keeping busy with other things, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Threat: Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Blocked Before Complete: I find myself pushing the memory away before I can fully recall it, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Amina lay in the dark of the bedroom, her husband’s quiet breathing a rhythm she had memorised over forty years of marriage. Even now, with his body warm beside her, she did not relax. Her ears tracked every creak of the house, every distant car, every settling of the floorboards. Sleep would come only when exhaustion finally pulled her under, usually in the hour before dawn. She had not spoken this to anyone. It was simply how she lived.

The abuse had happened more than three decades ago, with a man she had believed loved her. He had been charming until the evening he threw her to the ground in the community garden they tended together. She remembered the shock of the packed earth against her spine, the smell of turned soil and rotting leaves filling her nose as he kicked her ribs. She had tried to crawl away, but he followed, and that smell—damp earth, crushed grass—had become fused with the terror of being trapped and helpless. She left him after six months, but the memory had not left her.

In the years that followed, Amina built a careful life around avoidance without ever naming it that way. She married a gentle, steady man, but she had learned that safety came from never disagreeing. When he asked where she wanted to eat, she said whatever he preferred. When friends suggested a weekend trip, she agreed to whatever they wanted. People pleasing had become instinctive—if she gave no one a reason to be displeased, no one would hurt her. At home, she filled every hour with activity. There was always washing to fold, shelves to dust, vegetables to chop for the evening meal. If a moment of stillness found her, she immediately turned on the radio or picked up a crossword. Keeping her mind occupied meant the memory could not surface without warning, though it often did anyway. A whiff of damp soil from the garden outside the kitchen window, and suddenly she was back on the ground, the weight of him over her. She would shake her head sharply and focus on the frying pan, refusing to let the scene play out fully. She had become skilled at pushing the memory away before it could reach its conclusion.

Her world had shrunk without her noticing. There were only two places she felt safe: her bedroom and her kitchen. Anywhere else—a friend’s house, a shop, a medical waiting room—kept her scanning for exits and watching faces. When her husband travelled to visit his siblings, she could not sleep at all. Sleeping alone meant no one else listening for danger, and she would lie rigid until the alarm went off. The alertness followed her even into her own home. She would pause at the top of the stairs, listening, certain someone was in the basement. She checked locks twice before bed. She had come to believe that letting her guard down even for a moment was what bad things waited for.

Over the years, this vigilance had taken a toll on her marriage. Her husband had begun to ask why she never wanted to visit his family with him, why she always said yes to everything he suggested without offering her own opinion, why she seemed so exhausted all the time. She told him she was a light sleeper and that she liked a tidy house. She did not tell him that agreeing with him was the only way she knew to feel safe, or that her constant busyness was a wall she had built between herself and the smell of wet earth that could still bring her to her knees.

It was her daughter who finally insisted she see a doctor. Amina had flinched when a neighbour touched her shoulder unexpectedly, and her daughter had seen the look on her face—the flash of fear, the quick step backward. Two weeks later, Amina sat in a therapist’s office, her hands folded in her lap, ready to agree with whatever the therapist suggested. But instead, the therapist asked her what she wanted. For a long moment, Amina could not think of an answer. She had not been asked what she wanted in decades. What frightened her most was not the memory itself, but the possibility that if she let it come fully, she might never be able to push it away again. Still, something in her wanted to try.
